title: A Hyderabad Student's Rs 68,000 Satellite Receiver Brings Weather Images to Himalayan Villages
excerpt: Aagam Jain's SummitSathi pulls cloud images straight from weather satellites — no internet, no mobile signal. Three units will serve 10 villages in Himachal's Seraj valley, where networks fail in monsoon emergencies.
body:
• Aagam Jain, a Class 12 IB student at Indus International School, Hyderabad, has built SummitSathi, a satellite receiver that downloads cloud images directly from weather satellites — no internet or mobile network needed.
  • Each unit costs about Rs 68,000, built from readily available components; three units will serve 10 villages in Himachal Pradesh's Seraj valley, reaching more than 1,000 residents.
  • Three local operators have been trained to decode and interpret the satellite passes for their villages.
  • The receiver is not a cloudburst prediction system and does not replace India Meteorological Department warnings — it is an additional source of local weather information when networks fail.

When a monsoon cloudburst knocks out mobile networks in the mountains, the villages that most need weather information are the ones that cannot get it. A Hyderabad school student has built a device aimed at that gap. Aagam Jain, a Grade 12 International Baccalaureate student at Indus International School, Hyderabad, has designed and built SummitSathi, a satellite weather receiver that downloads cloud imagery directly from weather satellites without internet or cellular connectivity, The News Trust reported.

How it will be used

Three SummitSathi units will operate across 10 villages in the Seraj valley of Mandi district, Himachal Pradesh, reaching more than 1,000 residents. Each receiver is built from readily available, off-the-shelf components and costs approximately Rs 68,000. Three local residents have been trained as operators to decode and interpret the overhead satellite passes, giving the villages local weather information during severe monsoon weather and cellular network blackouts.

The limits are stated plainly by the developer. SummitSathi is not a cloudburst prediction system, not an automated forecast tool and not a substitute for India Meteorological Department advisories. It is a supplementary source: a way for a village to see the cloud picture for itself when the usual channels are down.

The student behind it

Jain, who developed the project after travelling in high-altitude regions vulnerable to extreme weather, has filed an Indian patent application as the sole inventor, and was scheduled to present the work at ECRS 2026, an international remote-sensing conference, from October 19 to 21, according to the project reports. His other work runs in the same direction: independent astronomy research on approximately 595 suspected exoplanets using software he wrote himself, a 24-month study of Hyderabad's night-sky brightness at 25 locations, and a self-published astrophotography book, A Window to the Universe, distributed to more than 350 students through his Summit Stargazer initiative. He also captains his school's athletics team and competes nationally in sprinting and hammer throw.

SummitSathi's premise is deliberately modest: not a new forecast, but a receiver a village can run itself, for about Rs 68,000, on the days the network disappears.
